title: Black stools in a minimally verbal 3-year-old

source.citation: Burman AN. A Case of Unwitnessed Ingestion: Highlighting the Diagnostic Challenge in High-Risk Patients. Cureus. 2025;17(11):e96362.

presentation.hpi: Brought in by his grandparents, whom he is visiting: for three days he has passed one dark, black, semi-formed stool a day and has complained intermittently of abdominal pain, from which he is easily distracted. No vomiting, reduced appetite, drooling, swallowing difficulty, cough, stridor or breathlessness. He is minimally verbal, so the history is limited. On further questioning he is known to eat non-food items, regularly including sand, and three days ago he came home from nursery with a dark blue-stained tongue, thought to be from ink or pigment.
pmh: Awaiting assessment for autism; minimally verbal and follows only a few commands
meds: Daily herbal multivitamin and probiotic supplements (limited diet)
presentation.social: Visiting his grandparents, who brought him in; attends nursery.

exam: Actively playing in the department; distressed by having observations taken
No acute abnormality: airway, breathing and circulation normal
Examination limited by his communication difficulties
Stool (photographed by family): black, semi-formed; consistent with melena or pigment staining

imaging.finding: 21.9 mm round radio-opaque object in the stomach with a halo sign; a second 9.4 mm radio-opaque object in the right iliac fossa. The film did not include the pelvis.

diagnosis.primary: Button battery ingestion (unwitnessed) with a 21.9 mm battery retained in the stomach and melena
differentials: Black stool from ingested pigment, iron or bismuth

management: Discussed with the regional pediatric surgical team and transferred within 190 minutes of triage
Endoscopic retrieval within 6 h of triage (rat-tooth, then Magill forceps); no significant tissue injury apart from mild erythema at the pylorus
Observed overnight and discharged with advice to return if symptoms persisted
outcome: Doing well since discharge; the melena resolved.
teachingPoints: Suspect unwitnessed foreign-body ingestion in young, nonverbal or developmentally delayed children, especially with pica, unexplained GI bleeding, food refusal, drooling or respiratory symptoms.

Image the whole tract, from nasopharynx to anus, ideally in two views; a halo (double-ring) outline on the frontal view and a step-off on the lateral view distinguish a button battery from a coin (thin batteries may lack the halo).
An esophageal button battery is an emergency: remove it immediately, ideally within 2 hours, because hydroxide generated at the negative pole causes liquefactive necrosis within hours.

Honey (from 1 year of age) or sucralfate can limit esophageal injury while removal of a recent ingestion (within 12 h) is arranged, without delaying it (National Capital Poison Center guideline); neither is indicated once the battery is known to be beyond the esophagus (ESPGHAN 2021 position paper).
Batteries beyond the esophagus usually pass, but a symptomatic child needs endoscopic removal and assessment for injury (ESPGHAN 2021 position paper).

questions.q: Given his history of eating non-food items, which imaging is most appropriate?
options: Radiographs from the nasopharynx to the anus
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
questions.explanation: For a suspected radio-opaque foreign body, radiographs should cover the whole tract from the nasopharynx to the anus, with a lateral view of any object, so that an esophageal battery or a second object is not missed; this child's single abdominal film omitted the pelvis. Ultrasound and CT are not first-line.

questions.q: What is the 21.9 mm gastric object most likely to be?
questions.extra: Abdominal radiograph: a 21.9 mm round radio-opaque object in the stomach whose edge shows a double-ring (halo) outline, and a 9.4 mm radio-opaque object in the right iliac fossa.
questions.explanation: A double-ring (halo) outline on the frontal view, with a step-off on the lateral view, is the classic sign of a button battery; a coin is a uniformly dense disc and a washer has a central hole. Stacked coins can mimic the halo, so treat it as a battery until proven otherwise.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.extra: Battery in the stomach; time of ingestion unknown (stools black for 3 days). Hemoglobin 113 g/L (reference 115–140); coagulation and renal function normal.
options: Discharge with a repeat radiograph in 7–14 days
Polyethylene glycol to speed passage, then stool checks
Honey every 10 minutes and overnight observation
questions.explanation: Most batteries beyond the esophagus pass, but this child is symptomatic (melena, abdominal pain, mild anemia) after an unknown, possibly prolonged exposure to a cell over 20 mm, so prompt endoscopic removal and assessment for injury are indicated (ESPGHAN 2021 position paper). Honey is for recent ingestions while an esophageal battery awaits removal, not for a gastric battery.

questions.q: Which scenario carries the greatest risk of severe injury after button battery ingestion?
options: A battery under 15 mm that has reached the colon
A 20 mm lithium cell lodged in the esophagus of a toddler
A zinc-air hearing-aid battery in a teenager's stomach
A battery passed in the stool within 24 hours
questions.explanation: Severe and fatal outcomes cluster in children under 5 with 20 mm-plus, 3-V lithium cells impacted in the esophagus, where hydroxide generated at the negative pole causes necrosis within about 2 hours and can lead to perforation, tracheoesophageal or aortoesophageal fistula and vocal cord paralysis. Small batteries beyond the esophagus usually pass without harm.

evidence.quote: The patient in question was a three-year-old boy awaiting assessment for autism and known to suffer from chronic constipation.
He was regularly taking multiple herbal vitamins and probiotic supplements due to a limited diet
Developmentally, he was minimally verbal and followed only a few commands, which posed difficulties with history taking and a thorough examination.
He was brought in by his grandparents, whom he was visiting at the time
with a three-day history of passing dark stool once daily (black semi-formed stool, no comment on offensive smell)
intermittent complaints of distractable abdominal pain
the patient attended without any history of vomiting, reduced appetite, distress, drooling, dysphagia, irritability, cough, stridor, or shortness of breath
it came to light that he had a history of ingesting non-food items. This included regularly consuming sand
three days prior, returning home from nursery with a dark blue-stained tongue, which was thought to possibly indicate ink/pigment ingestion
His initial observations were all normal, except for a heart rate of 158 beats per minute, likely due to his being actively playing in the department
distressed by having his observations taken
His initial examination showed no acute abnormalities; his airway, breathing, and circulation were normal, and he had no abdominal tenderness.
Patient's abnormal stool - appearances in keeping with melaena or black-stained stool
photographs taken by family members suggested this was likely melaena
a 21.9 mm round radio-opaque object in the stomach with a halo sign indicative of a button battery
a further 9.4 mm radio-opaque object in the right iliac fossa
The abdominal X-ray was of poor quality because it did not include the pelvis
Haemoglobin | 113 g/L | 115–140 g/L
Mean cell volume | 79.6 fL | 73-90 fL
Mean cell haemoglobin concentration | 325 g/L | 313–352 g/L
Platelet count | 292x10⁹/L
Prothrombin time | 11.1 seconds | 11–13.5 seconds
APTT | 27.8 seconds
Creatinine | 28 μmol/L | 23–37 μmol/L
Urea | 4.6 mmol/L | 2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Blood results immediately prior to transfer were normal, apart from mild anaemia, possibly acute
he was discussed with the local paediatric surgical team and transferred to their hospital within 190 minutes of triage
He underwent endoscopic retrieval within six hours of triage with successful removal of the button battery using rat tooth and then Magill forceps.
there was no significant tissue injury identified, apart from an area of mild erythema at the pylorus
He was observed overnight and discharged home with advice to return if he experiences ongoing symptoms.
Since then, he has been doing well, and his melaena has resolved.
